items.prose: A moving-average signal goes long when yesterday's close is above the mean of the last n closes. The starter version peeks at today's close and never rejects n = 0. Work red-green: write the three tests, watch them fail, then fix `ma_signal`.

state.caption: The 2-day mean at day i averages closes i − 1 and i; day i + 1 trades on it

items.question: Write the tests, see red, then fix `ma_signal` until they pass.

widget.starter:
import pytest


def ma_signal(closes, n):
    # Position for day t: 1 if close t - 1 is above the mean of closes t - n to t - 1, else 0.
    # Day t may use closes up to t - 1 only. Days before t = n are flat.
    # n below 1 must raise ValueError("n must be at least 1").
    out = []
    for t in range(len(closes)):
        window = closes[t - n + 1:t + 1]
        out.append(1 if t >= n - 1 and closes[t] > sum(window) / n else 0)
    return out

closes = [100.00, 104.00, 102.00, 107.00, 103.00, 108.00]

    pass  # parametrise over n = 2 and n = 3; write it before the fix

def test_last_close_moves_nothing():
    pass

def test_window_below_one_raises():
    pass

items.question: Which test ids does pytest report?

options.why: pytest builds ids from the values, not only row numbers. A number like −0.1 appears as itself.
A list is not written out. It is named by its parameter and row number, as `prices0`.
Each row is its own test with its own id.

feedback.correct: Lists get their name and row number; numbers appear as themselves.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about how pytest names a list value.

explain.text: pytest joins one piece per parameter with '-'. A list becomes its parameter name plus the row number, such as `prices0`. A number appears as itself, so −0.1 gives the double dash in `prices0--0.1`.

```python
CLOSES = [100.00, 110.00, 99.00, 108.90, 98.01]

def test_everything():
    expected = simple_returns(CLOSES)
    assert simple_returns(CLOSES) == expected
    CLOSES.append(107.81)
    assert max_drawdown(CLOSES) < 0
    with pytest.raises(Exception):

    assert CLOSES[-1] == 98.01
```

items.prose: You are fixing a reported bug test first. Your new test is written, and you have not changed the code yet.
items.question: Why run the new test before you fix the code?

options.text: To see it fail, which proves it can detect the bug
To measure how long the test takes
options.why: Timing is not the point. A red run shows the test reaches the bug.

options.text: To check the test has no typos
options.why: A typo would show up later too. The point is to watch the test fail for the reported reason.

options.text: There is no reason; you could run it after the fix
options.why: Run only after the fix, a pass cannot tell a working test from one that never touches the bug.

feedback.correct: Red first: a test that never failed has not shown it can catch the bug.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What would a pass after the fix prove on its own?

explain.text: Run only after the fix, a pass could mean the fix worked. It could also mean the test misses the bug. Seeing it fail on the old code rules out the second. Then green means the fix did the job.
